exhibitions.title: The Places We Keep: Holding Place, Holding Time
exhibitions.description:
In The Places We Keep, students reflect on their most cherished spaces—familiar domestic settings, shared public forums, secret hiding spots, culturally significant locations—during a 12-week course. Guided by instructors Shannon Eggleston and Michael Wilson, students investigate the impact that time, civic development, and unseen natural forces inevitably have on their treasured places’ appearances, functions, and associations, as seen through the lens of both intimacy and distance. The resulting images consider how spaces and moments of time can hold personal and collective significance, inviting viewers to consider how individual and communal identities and memories can shape environments.

In addition to the exhibition, students created time capsules to house film negatives of their selected works, and in some cases the displayed photographs themselves. These capsules, left at meaningful sites, offer a tangible archive for future audiences to discover. The Places We Keep is not only an exhibition, but also a gesture of continuity: a message from the present to those yet to come and an invitation to honor the places we cherish before they inevitably change.

exhibitions.title: The Sweep of Time, Beyond the Horizon
exhibitions.description:
A juried exhibition, The Sweep of Time, Beyond the Horizon emphasizes photography’s unique ability to hold two things at once: the instant and what endures beyond it. The horizon, central to the exhibition, functions as both a literal subject and a symbolic threshold—an opening into broader contexts of time, memory, and continuity. In this way, distance and perspective become the focus while also welcoming works that consider temporal scale and duration, creating a space where history and the future coexist. Some works attend to memory and generational connection, while others imagine what lies ahead. Together, they place the present moment within a wider trajectory.

The Sweep of Time, Beyond the Horizon offers a way of seeing that resists the urgency of the immediate. By presenting diverse lens-based works that embody continuity and expanded vision, the exhibition fosters reflection, patience, and a deeper sense of orientation within time.

exhibitions.title: This Land, Here We Dwell
exhibitions.venue: Northern Kentucky University School of the Arts Galleries
exhibitions.curator_line: Curated by Kelsey Nolin, Independent Curator
exhibitions.description: This Land, Here We Dwell focuses on contemporary photographers in the United States who engage with time and land as both subject and material. The featured artists incorporate meditations on the land and environment as part of their practice, encompassing historical ecologies, current climates, and imagined futures. Within their studies of the land, each artist also embraces time as a critical element of photographic language and integrates time as material, subject, and methodology. Artists employ long exposures and moving images, research-based practices, and ephemeral materials during repeated visits with their subjects. Based throughout the United States, these photographers unveil rich knowledge of the different ecosystems within the country and how these environments inform our daily lives.

exhibitions.title: This We Believe
exhibitions.description: What are the costs and consequences of allegiance? This We Believe explores the power and evolution of belief systems—religious, political, economic—and how adherence to and rejection of these ideologies has influenced our current global culture of divisiveness and polarization. From imagery of disillusionment and protest, to revelations of historical complexity and visions of transcending binary definitions of identity, the artworks featured question and critique unalloyed allegiance to creed or country.

exhibitions.title: Trent Davis Bailey: The North Fork
exhibitions.description:
In The North Fork, Trent Davis Bailey intertwines childhood memories with images and moments from family farms on Colorado’s Western Slope. “The North Fork” comes from the name locals use to broadly describe the agrarian valley in which they live, which is situated on Colorado’s Western Slope and irrigated by the North Fork of the Gunnison River.

In addition to The North Fork series, a selection of archival photographs depicting the same region is on view. Included are prints by two Farm Security Administration photographers, Russell Lee and Arthur Rothstein, as well as lesser-known photographers whose prints are held in the archives of a local historical society, weaving together past and present. Suggesting the arc of history in the region, as well as the artist’s long-standing connection with the place, this exhibition demonstrates how Bailey’s work connects with a photographic and historic lineage while also serving as a tool for self-discovery.

exhibitions.title: Trevor Paglen: the most merciful thing in the world
exhibitions.curator_line: Curated by Kevin Moore, Ph.D., FotoFocus Artistic Director and Curator
exhibitions.description:
Trevor Paglen operates at the crossroads of art, technology, and philosophy. His work explores image-making technologies as increasingly powerful animators of geopolitical exchange and arbiters of how we see our world. Balancing tensions between the visible and invisible, beauty and terror, Paglen reveals the ways digital imagery mimics traditional forms of representation while spawning unfamiliar and, at times, unsettling motifs.

His interest in images that are not based on human vision, but as logical outcomes of computational processes, stems from Paglen’s fascination with the sublime, an 18th-century philosophy of nature as both awe-inspiring and threatening. While considering Romantic paintings that visualized this concept, Paglen has asked: “What are the monsters in our skies now?” This reframing of the sublime, coined by theorist Hal Foster as the techno-sublime, no longer considers nature as the ominous threat but rather human-wielded technology such as spy satellites, Reaper drones, and rendition flights.

Trevor Paglen: the most merciful thing in the world features photography, video, and sculpture spanning a twenty-year period, presenting works that activate—through telescopic and computer vision—new ways of seeing the world while revealing what is designed to remain unseen within systems of surveillance or military power. The exhibition subtitle is borrowed from science fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft (1890–1937): “the most merciful thing in the world” is our ignorance, which ultimately protects us from fully comprehending the vast and terrifying universe. Across multiple distinct series, this exhibition examines how human interactions with technology— from telescopic views of military sites and the cosmos, to interactive facial-recognition technologies, to the darker prospects of AI-generated imagery and alternate-reality games—test the capacities of human perception and cognition.

exhibitions.title: True Body Project: Time is a Circle
exhibitions.description: Created by six youth artists in collaboration with filmmaker Andrea Sisson, True Body Project: Time is a Circle is a multi-channel film reflecting on the nature of time, memory, and identity, inspired by Alan Lightman’s much-loved book, Einstein’s Dreams. Youth artists ages, 16–20, create this film experience over seven weeks as part of The Well’s True Body Project and in collaboration with ArtWorks/1001 Colors’ Youth Apprentice Artist program. These artists collaboratively ponder their own sense of time while creating all aspects of a multi-channel film experience focused on the cartography of place and belonging. This dynamic meeting of time and place gives a haunting and hopeful view of our world from today’s future artists and leaders.

exhibitions.title: Unfolding Stories 2026: Stories from the RCCAM Collection
exhibitions.description:
Unfolding Stories traces the rich history of the Richard and Carole Cocks Art Museum’s (RCCAM) collection through the perspective of visual artists, art historians, dancers, and architects. From art historical research to experimental animation/video and mixed media installation, this expansive exhibition encompasses a wide array of studies, interpretations, and expressions by more than 60 artists, scholars, and students associated with Miami University.

Established in 1978, the RCCAM at Miami University hosts over 17,500 artworks in its permanent collection. The collaborators of Unfolding Stories engage in an in-depth exploration of the collection from pre-Columbian artifacts to contemporary art, including works by Eadweard Muybridge, Berenice Abbott, Steve Schapiro, Felice Beato, H. A. Sigg, William Douglas McGee, Philip Morsberger, Kara Walker, Judith Brown, Sam Gilliam, and Nancy Holt. The culmination of this multifaceted creative research is showcased through projection mapping events, a multimedia exhibition, and artist talks.

exhibitions.title: Unorthodocs
exhibitions.curator_line: Curated by Chris Stults, Associate Curator of Film/Video
exhibitions.description:
Celebrating its 10th anniversary, Unorthodocs at the Wexner Center for the Arts is an acclaimed annual film festival dedicated to innovative contemporary nonfiction filmmaking. The festival showcases emerging and established filmmakers, many of whom attend in person for post-screening conversations with audiences. The five-day festival features film screenings, filmmaker talks, and a mid-week reception that brings artists and audiences together.

Each year, Unorthodocs presents a diverse slate of local, regional, national, and international nonfiction films that foreground inventive storytelling, archival discoveries, and underrepresented voices. Over the past nine years, the festival has welcomed filmmakers from around the world—including Brazil, Morocco, Serbia, and South Africa—while also providing an important platform for filmmakers working closer to home.

Together, these perspectives offer Ohio audiences opportunities to engage directly with artists working across a wide range of cultural and geographic contexts. In an era dominated by streaming platforms, Unorthodocs remains a vital space for discovering independent documentary films on the big screen and for experiencing the evolving possibilities of nonfiction cinema.

exhibitions.title: Untwined/Interwoven
exhibitions.venue: Art Academy of Cincinnati: Pearlman Gallery
exhibitions.description:
Untwined/Interwoven considers the photograph as a fragment—memory as shards of glass, scraps of fabric, or prints sewn together. Faded due to time, memories are often fickle and unreliable in nature. What pieces can be collected, selected, and separated to tell personal and collective histories? This question highlights the ephemeral, impermanent, and fragmented nature of photography as a medium that translates memory into a solid entity and serves as a vessel for remembrance and storytelling.

Curated by students at the Art Academy of Cincinnati, artists Angela Kahoali’i Casagrande, Diana Noh, and Kaitlin Santoro investigate memories through lens-based and mixed media images and fragments. By collaging found materials with photographs, all three artists show their own unique vision of what it means to hold onto and mend lived experience. Their work serves as a metric to reach into the past and reflect, creating a space for distressed recollections of place and fractured dimensions of time.

exhibitions.title: Waiting to Be Seen
exhibitions.curator_line: Curated by Sandy Eichert, Resident Curator
exhibitions.description:
Waiting to be Seen pays tribute to the charged, chaotic, and deeply human theater of street life. Inspired by the spirit of Diane Arbus, the exhibition features street photography and photojournalism that documents drag performers, queer communities, clowns, bodybuilders, and everyday passersby in moments of unfiltered presence.

From the defiant joy of a sidewalk voguing battle to the quiet intimacy of public rituals, these images capture the unscripted drama of urban life. The work blurs the line between art and reportage, suggesting viewers see the street not just as a backdrop, but as a living, breathing character.

exhibitions.title: Wayfarers
exhibitions.curator_line: Curated by Virginia Volle, Arts Program Administrator
exhibitions.description: Instructor Steve Groh leads students by mapping out and documenting his journey in photography, ultimately encouraging his students to envision and illustrate their own paths. Wayfarers displays three views: Groh’s own path, illustrated through one-on-one sojourns with those significant to his development as artist and teacher; his current students’ work, imbued with their own histories and future longings; and former students’ photographs, evoking further introspections, hopes, and fears. Groh inspires each of his students to travel back into the past and forward into the unknown, and to capture key moments with dedication and heart. As fellow travelers of their own long roads, viewers can experience the personal expeditions of others through the lenses of “wayfarers” at different stages of their journeys.

exhibitions.title: Widline Cadet: Seremoni Disparisyon (Ritual [Dis]Appearance)
exhibitions.curator_line: Curated by Kristen Gaylord, Herzfeld Curator of Photography and Media Arts at the Milwaukee Art Museum
exhibitions.description:
Widline Cadet: Seremoni Disparisyon (Ritual [Dis]Appearance), the second presentation of the artist’s first solo museum exhibition in the United States, presents her acclaimed series exploring Black diasporic life through her family’s immigration from Haiti.

After leaving Haiti as a child, Cadet originally photographed her extended family to supplement the small number of images of her ancestors that had been passed down, counteracting both the physical separation from her home country and the loss of these relatives. But increasingly limited access to her family abroad inspired the artist to turn the camera on herself, as well as other Black women around her, creating a stand-in archive that explores absence through presence.

Seremoni Disparisyon addresses shared themes of immigration, including loss, aspiration, and memory, through the specificity of Cadet’s experiences. Many works contain concrete autobiographical details: family photographs and videos, personal belongings like the curtains her mother brought from Haiti, and Kreyòl titles drawn from actual conversations. Others stretch across distance and memory, like the photograph of a model in a gingham dress, a re-creation of the artist’s childhood school uniform. Although displaced from her original home, Cadet nevertheless finds echoes of it everywhere, such as the breeze-block architecture and bougainvillea flowers of her current residence, Los Angeles. This doubling recurs throughout Seremoni Disparisyon —building a dreamlike, proxy world inhabited by elements both real and imagined, experienced and missed.

This exhibition includes work from across the entire series, bringing together photographs, installation, and video to encompass the breadth of Cadet’s imagemaking practice and capacious approach to photography, including vinyl application, photo-sculpture hybrids, and multimedia presentations.

exhibitions.title: Witness to the Journey: Matt Herron and the Deep South, 1965
exhibitions.description:
Witness to the Journey: Matt Herron and the Deep South, 1965 presents a compelling selection of 28 black-and-white photographs by renowned civil rights photographer Matt Herron. This exhibition documents the historic Selma to Montgomery March for Voting Rights, a pivotal moment in American history that directly led to the passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Herron’s images capture the spirit, struggle, and triumph of the marchers—ordinary citizens, activists, and leaders—who walked 54 miles over five days to demand justice. The photographs reveal the diversity of participants, the role of music and federal protection, and the emotional highs and lows of the journey. The exhibition concludes with images reflecting the immediate impact of the Voting Rights Act and the ongoing fight for voter equity. By revisiting these images in 2026, America’s 250th anniversary, the exhibition encourages reflection on how far we’ve come and how far we still must go.

Presented in the Freedom Center’s Skirball Gallery, the exhibition will be accompanied by Herron’s personal effects, including his leather camera bag and hip carrier, contextualizing the photographs and the broader Civil Rights Movement. Selected images are sourced from an exhibition originally curated by Herron and now part of the Freedom Center’s museum collection, offering a powerful lens into the moral arc of history and the enduring pursuit of justice.

events.title: Walking for A Second Look
events.description:
This two-hour walk will begin at the Over-the-Rhine Museum at 3 West McMicken Avenue to briefly discuss the exhibition, Second Look: Danny Ransohoff’s Cityscapes Through New Eyes. From there, with copies of Danny Ransohoff’s historic photos in hand, the group will walk to five of the locations featured in the show. Once oriented in each spot, we will discuss change over time by comparing the photograph of the past and present before our eyes. We may even begin to imagine the neighborhood’s future. This walk will be led by University of Cincinnati Research Assistant Professor of History, Anne Delano Steinert.

Additional Information: Participants should come dressed for the weather and expect moderate exercise. Please RSVP to hello@otrmuseum.org to stay informed in case of inclement weather.

participants.name: Lindsay Albert
participants.title: Program Manager, KADIST
participants.bio: Lindsay Albert is a curator and arts producer based in San Francisco, CA, currently serving as Program Manager at KADIST. Her career spans the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, McEvoy Foundation for the Arts, and Minnesota Street Project. Albert has curated notable exhibitions including Makeshift Memorials, Small Revolutions presented at KADIST and the Blaffer Art Museum (Houston, TX), Natural Fictions at The Carnegie (Covington, KY), and produced solo presentations by Indira Allegra, Leila Weefer, and Ragnar Kjartansson. In 2023, Albert co-founded staircase, an alternative project space exclusively presenting female and non-binary artists in the Bay Area. Her curatorial practice is rooted in Romantic conceptualism and the poetics of memory, and the intersection of art and social discourse. (Photo Credit: Jenna Garrett)

participants.name: Joshua Berg
participants.title: Artist
participants.bio: Joshua Berg is a photographer based in Covington, KY, at the confluence of the Ohio and Licking Rivers. Bound by the rhythms of two rivers, his work centers on the idea of home and the experience of living and growing up in the Midwest. His books and photographs explore the impossibility of untethering the body from place, and the endless dialogue of unraveling the actual. (Photo Credit: Brian Pfaff)
events: Conversation with Artists Joshua Berg, Heesoo Kwon, and Phillip Maisel moderated by Curator Lindsay Albert

participants.name: Kristen Gaylord
participants.title: Herzfeld Curator of Photography and Media Arts at the Milwaukee Art Museum
participants.bio: Kristen Gaylord is the Herzfeld Curator of Photography and Media Arts at the Milwaukee Art Museum (MAM), where she recently organized Widline Cadet’s first solo exhibition at an American museum (2026) and Erin Shirreff: Permanent Drafts (2025), and serves as site curator for the Victoria and Albert Museum’s Arresting Beauty: Julia Margaret Cameron (2024). This year she opened Beneath the Surface: Mining and American Photography, a major survey of the relationship between photography and extractive industries in the United States from the 1840s until today, co-curated for the National Gallery of Art and currently on tour. Previously, Gaylord was a photography curator at the Amon Carter Museum of American Art, where she worked with artists including Stephanie Syjuco and Camille Utterback and brought landmark surveys of An-My Lê and Christina Fernandez to Fort Worth. Additionally, she co-organized Moving Pictures: Karl Struss and the Rise of Hollywood (2024), whose catalogue won the Deutscher Fotobuchpreis. Gaylord also held multiple curatorial roles at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, NY, where she contributed to exhibitions and publications including Stephen Shore (2017); Arbus Friedlander Winogrand: New Documents, 1967 (2017); and Ocean of Images: New Photography 2015. She holds an M.A. and a Ph.D. in art history from the Institute of Fine Arts at New York University. (Photo Credit: Ciara Elle Bryant)

participants.name: Elijah Howe
participants.title: Photographer
participants.bio: Elijah Howe is a photographer who currently lives and works in Felton, CA. His work focuses on the fragmentary nature of photography and people’s relationships with one another, as well as their relationship with the land. Howe’s work explores quiet transitionary spaces in the landscape and the unsettling melancholy of the human condition.
events: In the Interest of Time Gallery Tour

participants.name: Daniel Immerwahr
participants.title: Bergen Evans Professor in the Humanities at Northwestern University
participants.bio: Daniel Immerwahr is Bergen Evans Professor in the Humanities at Northwestern University, where he teaches both United States and global history. He is a contributing writer at The New Yorker, and has written two award-winning books, Thinking Small (Harvard, 2015) and the New York Times bestselling How to Hide an Empire (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2019), which has been translated into nine languages. Immerwahr’s writing has appeared in the New York Times, The Atlantic, Harper’s, The New Republic, The Guardian, the New York Review of Books, The Nation, Foreign Policy, and Slate. He lives in Rogers Park, Chicago.

participants.name: Julie Renée Jones
participants.title: Artist
participants.bio:
Julie Renée Jones is a photographic-based artist and educator currently living in Dayton, OH. Her work explores autobiographical narratives related to familial myth and matrescence, using the camera as a tool to reveal magic residing within the everyday and memory as a medium for approaching the unknown.

Her work has been exhibited extensively across the United States and internationally, and has been published in National Geographic and the British Journal of Photography. A selection of images from her series Hold Still is featured in Eye Mama: Poetic Truths of Home and Motherhood published by teNeues. She is a recipient of numerous awards and grants in support of her work, including two Ohio Arts Council’s Individual Excellence Awards.
events: In the Interest of Time Gallery Tour

participants.name: Heesoo Kwon
participants.title: Artist
participants.bio: Heesoo Kwon is a multimedia artist and educator based in San Francisco and Los Angeles. Having initiated the autobiographical feminist religion and speculative universe Leymusoom in 2017, she has exhibited internationally for nearly a decade. Kwon’s work is held in the permanent collections of the Cantor Arts Center at Stanford University, KADIST, Huis Marseille, and the University of California Irvine Langson Orange County Museum of Art, and has been covered by Hyperallergic, Artforum, Rhizome, the Brooklyn Rail, and e-flux, among others. (Photo Credit: Breno Aragon)
events: Conversation with Artists Joshua Berg, Heesoo Kwon, and Phillip Maisel moderated by Curator Lindsay Albert

participants.name: Elizabeth Leitzell
participants.title: Photographer and Short Filmmaker
participants.bio: Elizabeth Leitzell is a photographer, short-film maker, and editor based in the Greater Philadelphia Area. On most days, you’ll find her working on collaborations with visual artists, musicians, authors, start-ups, and non-profit institutions in the arts, social services, and sciences. She believes in using the power of image-based narratives for social change. Through a free exploration of color, composition, listening, and emotion, Leitzell hopes her work can support building new systems of cooperation, reconciliation, and reorganization. (Photo Credit: Kyle Struve)
events: Conversation with Nathaniel M. Stein and Elizabeth Leitzell

participants.name: Phillip Maisel
participants.title: Artist
participants.bio: Phillip Maisel utilizes site-informed materials to create sculpture, collage, video, and photographic objects. His work often subverts expectations of photographic space, destabilizing the viewer’s visual literacy. He received his M.F.A. from the California College of the Arts in San Francisco and his B.S. in Psychology from McGill University in Montreal, Canada. Maisel has presented solo exhibitions at the Chiquita Room, Barcelona, Spain; Gregory Lind Gallery, San Francisco, CA; Nazarian / Curcio (formerly Shulamit Nazarian), Los Angeles, CA; and DOCUMENT, Chicago, IL. He has exhibited at The William Benton Museum of Art at the University of Connecticut; the University of New Mexico, Taos; and the deCordova Sculpture Park and Museum, Boston, MA. His book, Two Concrete Things, received the ArtsLibris-Fundació Banc Sabadell Award in 2021. His work is included in the KADIST collection, as well as the High Museum, Atlanta, GA.
events: Conversation with Artists Joshua Berg, Heesoo Kwon, and Phillip Maisel moderated by Curator Lindsay Albert

participants.name: Robyn Moore
participants.title: Photomedia-based Artist
participants.bio:
Robyn Moore is a photomedia-based artist living and working in eastern Kentucky. Her work explores how alternative and experimental photographic processes can reveal the unseen worlds around us, while her research investigates deep time, biosemiotics, geology, paleontology, phenomenology, and the ways in which images can help us facilitate understanding of and solidarity with other forms of life.

Moore’s work has been exhibited widely, including at the Jubilee Fifth International Print Biennale, Yerevan, Armenia; the South Australian Museum, Adelaine, Australia; Gold Street Studios Gallery, Victoria, Australia; the Centre for Print Research, Bristol, England; Houston Center for Photography, Soho Photo Gallery, New York, NY; The Halide Project, Philadelphia, PA; The Image Flow Photography Center, San Anselmo, CA; and Manhattan Graphics Center, New York, NY. Recent honors include selection as the 2024 South Arts Southern Prize and State Fellowship recipient for Kentucky, the 2025 Uncommon Art Residency Award at the Teton Art Lab in Jackson, WY, and a Great Meadows Foundation Artist Professional Development Grant. Moore’s work won the professional series alternative processes category at the 23rd Julia Margaret Cameron Awards for Women Photographers.

Moore holds a Ph.D. in Visual Arts from the University of Sydney and an M.F.A. in Photography and Experimental Film from the School of the Museum of Fine Arts at Tufts University. She is currently an Associate Professor of Photography at Morehead State University in Morehead, KY.
events: In the Interest of Time Gallery Tour

participants.name: Osamu James Nakagawa
participants.title: Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor at Indiana University
participants.bio: Osamu James Nakagawa was born in New York City, raised in Tokyo, and returned to the United States at age fifteen, when he moved to Houston, TX. His artistic practice moves fluidly between the personal and political, shaped by his transnational experience in both Japan and the United States. Nakagawa received his M.F.A. from the University of Houston in 1993 and is currently the Ruth N. Halls Distinguished Professor of Art at Indiana University Bloomington. Nakagawa is the recipient of numerous honors, including the 2009 Guggenheim Fellowship. His work has been exhibited nationally and internationally and is held in major public collections such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, NY; the George Eastman Museum, Rochester, NY; the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum; the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, TX; the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; and others. He is represented by PGI, Tokyo. (Photo Credit: Elaine Miller)

participants.name: Trevor Paglen
participants.title: Artist
participants.location: New York, NY and San Francisco, CA
participants.bio:
Paglen has had solo exhibitions at the Smithsonian Museum of American Art, Washington D.C.; Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh, PA; Fondazione Prada, Milan, Italy; the Barbican Centre, London, UK; Vienna Secession, Austria; and Protocinema Istanbul, Turkey; and participated in group exhibitions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, NY; the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Tate Modern, London, England; and numerous other venues.

Paglen has launched an artwork into distant orbit around Earth in collaboration with Creative Time and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), contributed research and cinematography to the Academy Award-winning film Citizenfour (2014), and created a radioactive public sculpture for the exclusion zone in Fukushima, Japan.

Paglen is the author of several books and many articles on subjects including experimental geography, artificial intelligence, state secrecy, military symbology, photography, and visuality. Paglen’s work has been profiled in the New York Times, The New Yorker,The Wall Street Journal, Wired, Financial Times, Artforum, and Aperture. In 2014, he received the Electronic Frontier Foundation’s Pioneer Award and, in 2016, he won the Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize. Paglen was named a MacArthur Fellow in 2017.

In March 2026, Paglen was named the winner of the LG Guggenheim Award. Paglen’s sixth book, How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI, was released by Verso Books in the same year.

Paglen holds a B.A. from the University of California, Berkeley, an M.F.A. from the Art Institute of Chicago, and a Ph.D. in Geography from the University of California, Berkeley. (Photo Credit: Michael Avedon)

participants.name: Jordanne Renner
participants.title: Multidisciplinary Artist
participants.bio: Jordanne Renner is a multidisciplinary portrait artist that primarily works within large format film photography, figurative sculpture, mixed media painting, public art, and installation. The notion of self, culture of place, the body and landscape, what we eat, and the psychology of memory are recurring topics of investigation in her work, as well as the idea of the photograph as an object. Split between the Midwest and the East Coast, Renner divides her time between studio practice, community endeavors, and teaching. She is a member of the National League of American Pen Women and the Society for Photographic Education, and is the Creative Wild of Gallery Palindroma & the ArtLab located in the Lower Hudson Valley.

participants.name: Paul Mpagi Sepuya
participants.title: Artist and Professor
participants.bio: Paul Mpagi Sepuya is a Los Angeles-based artist working in photography. He is known for his New York portrait series from the early 2000s, later moving into studio-based projects that question and complicate questions of authorship, the visualization of race and sexuality, and the structures of the photographic medium. Sepuya’s work has been acquired by the Getty Museum, Los Angeles, CA; Los Angeles County Museum of Art; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; The Museum of Modern Art, New York, NY; the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, NY; the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, NY; Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam; Tate Modern, London, England; the Victoria and Albert Museum, United Kingdom; and others. Solo museum exhibitions include Fotomuseum Amsterdam, PHOXXI at Deichtorhallen Hamburg, Germany; and surveys at the Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis, MO, and Nottingham Contemporary, United Kingdom. Focus. Desire., a survey of work from 2005–2025 was presented in 2026 at Fotomuseum Winterthur, Switzerland, and the Sprengel Museum in Hannover, Germany. His work has been covered and published in Artforum, Aperture, The New Yorker, The New York Times, Los Angeles Times, Art Review, Frieze, and Art in America. Sepuya is a Professor in Visual Arts and M.F.A. Program Director at the University of California San Diego, where he has taught since 2019.

participants.name: Shelby Sinclair
participants.title: Assistant Professor of African and African American Studies and History at the University of Virginia
participants.bio: Shelby Sinclair is a historian of the 19th and 20th century United States and Caribbean. She specializes in histories of the U.S. empire, military occupation, gender, and visual culture in the Caribbean and its diasporas. Her current book project explores Haitian women’s lives and labors during the 19-year U.S. military occupation of Haiti (1915–1934). (Photo Credit: Raisa Chowdhury).

participants.name: Nathaniel M. Stein
participants.title: Curator of Photography at the Cincinnati Art Museum
participants.bio: Nathaniel M. Stein, Ph.D., is Curator of Photography at the Cincinnati Art Museum (CAM). Stein earned degrees in art history from Wesleyan University and Brown University, where his doctoral research focused on the history of photography in India. He has organized exhibitions of historical and contemporary photography—including presentations in Cincinnati of the works of David Hartt and John Edmonds, Sohrab Hura, Gillian Wearing, the Kamoinge Workshop, and Hank Willis Thomas—and led the formation of the CAM’s Nancy Rexroth Collection. Recent publications include The Natural World (2022), The Levee: A Photographer in the American South (2020), and Interference: Andre Bradley and Paul Anthony Smith (2017), as well as contributions to Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in the Arts of South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Himalayan Region (2022). Prior to arriving in Cincinnati, Stein held curatorial positions at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and the Rhode Island School of Design Museum. Locally, he serves on the ArtsWave Pride Steering Committee. (Photo Credit: Tim Tiebout)

participants.name: Joseph Vitone
participants.title: Photographer
participants.bio: Joe Vitone is a documentary fine art photographer and educator. His work consists of large format portraiture and landscape in the United States, as well as panoramic and other views examining cultures abroad. He is Professor of Photocommunications at St. Edward’s University in Austin, TX, where he teaches both traditional and digital photography along with electronic media. He has received a National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship in Photography and was a Fulbright scholar in Costa Rica, as well as a Fulbright Specialist in the Apulia region of southern Italy. In Italy, Vitone’s work centered around small-scale, family-based agriculture and the evidence of place and culture in the urban area. In addition to presentations given in the United States, he has lectured on his photography in Australia, China, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam. His work has been exhibited at a number of venues including solo exhibitions at the Hungarian Museum of Photography, Kecskemét, Hungary; the Akron Art Museum, OH; and the Instituto Cultural Peruano Norteamericano, Lima, Peru. His work is held in a number of collections including the Cleveland Museum of Art, OH; the Center for Creative Photography at the University of Arizona, Tucson; the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, TX; the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest, Hungary; and the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, Washington, D.C. (Photo credit: Dylan Vitone)

participants.name: Lynn Whitney
participants.title: Associate Professor Emeritus
participants.bio:
Lynn Whitney is a large format black-and-white film photographer working in the documentary tradition. Her photographs illuminate timeless questions central to the human search for meaning and purpose, grounded by the landscape and animals. Through diverse, but universally connected subject matter including soldiers in the military, sisters in the convent, family members, farmers, and birders, Whitney’s work addresses the mysterious air we share in community with one another.

Whitney earned her B.A. in American Culture Studies from Boston University, her B.F.A. in Photography from the Massachusetts College of Art and Design, and her M.F.A. from Yale School of Art. Her monograph, Lake Erie (2023) was published by Kehrer Verlag, Heidelberg, Germany, and a monograph featuring her convent photographs, published by Dust Collective, will be available early 2027.

Whitney has received commissions from the Toledo Museum of Art and The George Gund Foundation in Cleveland, and an Individual Artist Grant from the Ohio Arts Council. Her work is in the collections of the Toledo Museum of Art, OH; The George Gund Foundation, Cleveland, OH; the Museum of Contemporary Photography at Columbia College Chicago Midwest Photographers Project, IL; the Cleveland Clinic, OH; Ohio Humanities; Southeast Center for Photographic Studies, Daytona Beach, FL; and Yale University, New Haven, CT.

Whitney is Associate Professor Emeritus of Photography at Bowling Green State University, where she served as Photography area head in the School of Art for over thirty years. She now lives in Northwest Ohio. (Photo Credit: Kevin Vereecke)

participants.name: Carmen Winant
participants.title: Artist and Roy Lichtenstein Chair of Studio Art at the Ohio State University
participants.bio: Carmen Winant is an artist and the Roy Lichtenstein Chair of Studio Art at the Ohio State University. Her work utilizes archival and authored photographs to examine feminist care networks, with particular emphasis on intergenerational, multiracial, and sometimes transnational coalition building. Winant’s recent projects have been shown at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, NY; Muzeum Sztuki Nowoczesnej, Warsaw, Poland; the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, NY; the Minneapolis Institute of Art, MN; SculptureCenter, Queens NY; Wexner Center for the Arts, Columbus, OH; the Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston, MA; the Cleveland Museum of Art, OH; and el Museo Universitario Arte Contemporáneo, Mexico City, Mexico. Winant’s artist’s books include My Birth (2018), Notes on Fundamental Joy (2019), Instructional Photography: Learning How To Live Now (2021), Arrangements (2022), A Brand New End: Survival and Its Pictures (2022), and The Last Safe Abortion (2024). Winant is a 2019 Guggenheim Fellow in photography, a 2020 Foundation of Contemporary Arts Artist Honoree, and a 2021 American Academy of Arts and Letters award recipient. She is also a community organizer, prison educator, and mother. (Photo Credit: Jordan Weitzman)
